pr.title: Retire RC4 cipher support in SSH
pr.body:
`BaseRC4Cipher.init` currently initializes RC4 with the supplied key, and `SshBuilder.setUpDefaultCiphers` offers Arcfour variants by default. RVSec reported that the `SecretKeySpec` call uses `ARCFOUR`, which its rule rejects. RFC 8758 prohibits Arcfour and RC4 in SSH, including the RFC 4345 variants.

I changed initialization to clear the existing cipher and throw, and removed the Arcfour factories from the defaults while retaining the other ciphers and their availability checks. This also removes the reported `Cipher` transformation violation in `init`. Peers that support only RC4 will no longer negotiate with the default configuration.

I chose to retire RC4 support rather than retain interoperability with peers that require it.

reviews.body:
Read this carefully — the fix is right, and the delegate approach is the cleanest way to do it.

**Context for anyone reading this later:** `trustAllCerts` is Feeder's user-opt-in helper for self-hosted servers with weird cert setups (self-signed, custom CA, mismatched hostname). The tightening here doesn't change what it accepts on the trust side — it changes what protocols the resulting `SSLSocketFactory` will speak. `SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")` on Android/JVM initialises the context correctly but leaves legacy TLSv1/TLSv1.1 (and, historically, SSLv2/v3) in each socket's `enabledProtocols`. `droidbot:dfs_naive` caught that.

What lands:

- `ProtocolFilteringSslSocketFactory` wraps every socket the delegate creates, then strips anything matching `SSL*`, `TLSv1`, `TLSv1.0`, `TLSv1.1` from `enabledProtocols`. What survives is TLS 1.2/1.3, which is exactly the tool's expectation.
- `filterLegacyTlsProtocols` throws `IOException` if the filter would empty the array — fail-secure rather than silently disable TLS entirely. Good.
- Wrapping is preferred over calling `SSLContext.getInstance("TLSv1.3")` because Android's min-API surface still varies on TLS 1.3 availability, and the delegate model keeps `NoSuchAlgorithmException` handling out of hot paths.
- All seven `createSocket` overloads are covered, including the `(socket, host, port, autoClose)` layered variant that OkHttp actually uses. If any of those had been missed, the wrapper would silently return an un-filtered socket for that code path.
- The `configure` closer-on-failure block preserves the filtering exception rather than swallowing it under a `close()` failure. Nice detail.

Small observations, non-blocking:

- `isLegacyTlsProtocol` uses `ignoreCase = true` — matches historical `TLSv1` vs `TLSv1.0` naming quirks across JDK vendors, so this is defensive not paranoid.
- The added androidTest exercises the filter directly; a wider integration test asserting a real TLSv1.2-only handshake would be nice-to-have but almost certainly not worth the emulator/network setup for one legacy edge case.

LGTM from a read-through.

Thanks for the contribution and for the detailed write-up!

As far as I can tell, this finding is a false positive for the OkHttp path. OkHttp already rejects TLS 1.1 and older by default, so filtering the protocols on the socket ourselves doesn't change anything.

In OkHttp 5.5.0 (the version we use):

- OkHttpClient uses DEFAULT_CONNECTION_SPECS = listOf(ConnectionSpec.MODERN_TLS, ConnectionSpec.CLEARTEXT) (OkHttpClient.kt).
- MODERN_TLS only allows TlsVersion.TLS_1_3 and TlsVersion.TLS_1_2. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are only in COMPATIBLE_TLS, which you have to opt into explicitly (ConnectionSpec.kt).
- Before every handshake, ConnectionSpec.apply() intersects sslSocket.enabledProtocols with those versions and sets the result on the socket. That's the same filtering this PR adds by hand.

We don't override connectionSpecs anywhere, so the default applies. The generic "TLS" argument to SSLContext.getInstance() is fine here: it picks the provider, and the protocol versions are then restricted per socket.

Thanks for checking this so carefully — you're right. With OkHttp 5.5.0 and no `connectionSpecs` override, `MODERN_TLS` already limits every socket to TLS 1.2/1.3 before the handshake, so the wrapper only repeats what OkHttp does. RVSec's rule only looks at the literal passed to `SSLContext.getInstance` and can't see OkHttp's per-socket filtering, so this is a false positive for the OkHttp path. I'll close the PR — sorry for the noise, and thanks for the clear explanation.
